If any one of the five or more persons who are conjointly committing dacoity commits murder in so doing, every one of those persons shall be punishable with death or imprisonment for life.
forbidden_points: Dacoity can be committed by fewer than five persons.
The punishment for dacoity is always death.

notes: Punishment query. Section 310.

query: What is the punishment for criminal breach of trust?

gold_references.label: Section 316
gold_references.role: definition and punishment for criminal breach of trust

required_points: Section 316(2) provides that whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
Section 316(3) provides that a carrier, wharfinger, or warehouse-keeper who commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.
Section 316(4) provides that a clerk or servant who commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

Section 316(5) provides that a public servant or professional (banker, merchant, etc.) who commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to ten years, and fine.
forbidden_points: The punishment for criminal breach of trust is always imprisonment for life.
Criminal breach of trust has a uniform punishment regardless of the capacity of the offender.

notes: Punishment query. Section 316 has tiered punishments based on capacity.

query: What is the punishment for cheating?

gold_references.label: Section 318
gold_references.role: definition and punishment for cheating

required_points: Section 318 provides that whoever cheats shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

Whoever cheats knowing that they are likely to cause wrongful loss to a person whose interest they were legally bound to protect shall be punished with imprisonment up to five years, or fine, or both.
Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces delivery of property or causes damage may attract higher punishment.
forbidden_points: The punishment for cheating is always imprisonment for life.
Cheating by personation has the same punishment as ordinary cheating.

notes: Punishment query. Section 318 has tiered punishments.

query: What is the punishment for false evidence?

gold_references.label: Section 229
gold_references.role: punishment for giving or fabricating false evidence

acceptable_references.label: Section 230
acceptable_references.reason: provides enhanced punishment for false evidence intending to procure capital conviction

required_points: Section 229(1) provides that whoever intentionally gives false evidence in any stage of a judicial proceeding, or fabricates false evidence for use in a judicial proceeding, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description up to seven years, and fine up to ten thousand rupees.
Section 229(2) provides that giving or fabricating false evidence in a non-judicial proceeding is punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine up to five thousand rupees.
optional_points: Section 230 provides for enhanced punishment of imprisonment for life or up to ten years where false evidence is given intending to procure conviction for a capital offence.
forbidden_points: All false evidence is punishable with a fixed seven-year sentence.
False evidence in non-judicial proceedings is not an offence.

notes: Punishment query. Section 229 with two tiers.

query: What is the punishment for criminal intimidation?

gold_references.label: Section 351
gold_references.role: definition and punishment for criminal intimidation

required_points: Section 351(2) provides that whoever commits criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Section 351(3) provides that if the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, destruction of property by fire, commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life or up to seven years, or to impute unchastity to a woman, the punishment is imprisonment up to seven years, or fine, or both.
Section 351(4) provides an additional two years if the threat is made by anonymous communication or with concealment of identity.
forbidden_points: The punishment for all criminal intimidation is always seven years.
Criminal intimidation requires physical violence.

notes: Punishment query. Section 351 has tiered punishments.

query: Someone pointed a knife at me and took my phone. What offence is this?

gold_references.label: Section 309
gold_references.role: robbery - theft or extortion using threat of instant hurt

acceptable_references.label: Section 303
acceptable_references.reason: theft is the underlying offence

acceptable_references.label: Section 304
acceptable_references.reason: snatching may be discussed depending on facts

required_points: Taking property by putting a person in fear of instant hurt (pointing a knife) can amount to robbery under Section 309.
Pointing a knife is legally relevant as it suggests a threat of instant hurt.
Theft is robbery if the offender causes or attempts to cause fear of instant hurt in order to commit the theft.
The final classification depends on facts proved.
optional_points: The answer may mention theft as the underlying offence.
forbidden_points: This is only simple theft with no robbery issue.
The punishment is guaranteed without knowing the full facts.

notes: Scenario query. Should identify robbery per Section 309.

query: Someone borrowed my phone and never returned it. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 316
gold_references.role: criminal breach of trust - entrusted property dishonestly converted

acceptable_references.label: Section 314
acceptable_references.reason: dishonest misappropriation may also be relevant if possession was originally innocent

wrong_references.label: Section 303
wrong_references.reason: theft is not applicable as the property was handed over with consent

required_points: When a person is entrusted with property and dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to their own use, it constitutes criminal breach of trust under Section 316.
Mere non-return may not automatically prove dishonest intent; the facts must be examined.
Theft under Section 303 does not apply because the property was handed over with consent.
optional_points: Criminal misappropriation under Section 314 may also be relevant depending on facts.
forbidden_points: This is definitely theft under Section 303.
Punishment is certain without further facts.

notes: Scenario query. Section 316 is the primary applicable provision.

query: I accidentally hit a person with my car while reversing. What can happen under BNS?

gold_references.label: Section 125
gold_references.role: rash or negligent act endangering life or personal safety

acceptable_references.label: Section 18
acceptable_references.reason: accident exception may apply if the act was lawful, careful, and without criminal intention or knowledge

acceptable_references.label: Section 106
acceptable_references.reason: causing death by rash or negligent act applies if death resulted

acceptable_references.label: Section 281
acceptable_references.reason: rash driving or riding on a public way may apply if the reversing happened on a public way

wrong_references.label: Section 103
wrong_references.reason: murder requires intention or knowledge; pure accident does not attract Section 103

required_points: If no death results but danger or hurt was caused by a rash or negligent act, Section 125 may apply.
If the act was truly accidental without criminal intention or knowledge, and with proper care and caution, Section 18 (accident exception) may apply.
optional_points: If death results from a rash or negligent act, Section 106 may apply.
The final determination depends on whether the act was rash or negligent.
forbidden_points: This amounts to murder under Section 103.
An accident always results in no liability.

notes: Scenario query. Section 125 is primary because death is not stated; Section 106 applies only if death occurs, and Section 18 may apply if truly accidental.

query: A person hit me first and I hit back to protect myself. Is it a crime?

gold_references.label: Section 34
gold_references.role: things done in private defence are not offences

gold_references.label: Section 35
gold_references.role: right of private defence of body

acceptable_references.label: Section 37
acceptable_references.reason: restrictions on the right of private defence

required_points: Under Section 34, nothing done in the exercise of the right of private defence is an offence.
Section 35 provides every person the right to defend their own body against an offence affecting the human body.
The right is limited; it cannot extend beyond what is necessary for defence, and there must not be time to seek public authority protection (Section 37).
optional_points: Whether this specific situation qualifies depends on the nature of the attack, the force used in retaliation, and whether it was necessary.
forbidden_points: Hitting back to protect oneself is always a crime.
Private defence permits any degree of force in retaliation.

notes: Scenario query. Should identify private defence under Section 34/35 with proper caveats.

query: A child below seven years damaged someone's property. Is the child liable?

gold_references.label: Section 20
gold_references.role: act of child under seven years is not an offence

required_points: Under Section 20 of BNS, nothing is an offence done by a child under seven years of age.
Therefore, a child below seven years has no criminal liability under BNS regardless of the act.
optional_points: Civil liability of parents or guardians for property damage may arise under civil law, but that is outside BNS.
forbidden_points: The child can be punished if the act was wilful.
The child is criminally liable because property damage is a serious offence.

notes: Scenario query applying Section 20.

query: A person with unsound mind committed an act that caused harm. How does BNS treat this?

gold_references.label: Section 22
gold_references.role: act of person of unsound mind not an offence if incapable of knowing nature or wrongfulness

acceptable_references.label: Section 36
acceptable_references.reason: others may still exercise right of private defence against such a person

required_points: Under Section 22, if a person at the time of the act, by reason of unsoundness of mind, was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law, the act is not an offence.
The unsoundness of mind must exist at the time of the act and must have rendered the person incapable; mere mental illness is not sufficient.
optional_points: Under Section 36, other persons may still exercise the right of private defence against acts by a person of unsound mind.
forbidden_points: A person with unsound mind can never be held criminally liable.
Unsoundness of mind at any time automatically excuses any act.

notes: Scenario query applying Section 22.

query: Someone forced me at gunpoint to help commit a crime. Will I still be punished?

gold_references.label: Section 32
gold_references.role: act compelled by threats of instant death - defence available except for murder

required_points: Section 32 provides that except for murder and offences against the State punishable with death, nothing is an offence done by a person compelled by threats that reasonably cause apprehension of instant death.
If the offence committed was murder or an offence against the State punishable with death, the defence under Section 32 is not available.
The person must not have voluntarily placed themselves in the situation by which they became subject to such constraint.
optional_points: The person must show that the threat was of instant death and that the apprehension was reasonable.
forbidden_points: Being forced at gunpoint always provides a complete defence regardless of the offence.
There is no defence available for acts done under compulsion.

notes: Scenario query applying Section 32. Murder exception is critical.

query: I injured someone while trying to stop a theft. Can private defence apply?

gold_references.label: Section 35
gold_references.role: right of private defence extends to property against theft

acceptable_references.label: Section 34
acceptable_references.reason: foundational provision for private defence

acceptable_references.label: Section 42
acceptable_references.reason: right of private defence of property does not extend to causing death in non-specified cases

acceptable_references.label: Section 37
acceptable_references.reason: sets restrictions on the right of private defence

acceptable_references.label: Section 41
acceptable_references.reason: private defence of property extends to causing death only in specified cases

required_points: Section 35 provides the right to defend property against theft, which includes causing harm to the offender.
The harm caused must not exceed what is necessary and must remain within the restrictions of Section 37.
The right of private defence of property does not ordinarily extend to causing death unless the act falls under the categories in Section 41 (robbery, house-breaking after sunset, etc.).
optional_points: If the theft did not involve a threat to life, the right may not extend to causing grievous hurt or death.
forbidden_points: Private defence can never apply to stopping a theft.
Any injury caused while stopping a theft is automatically excused.

notes: Scenario query. Private defence of property applies but with restrictions.

query: Someone entered my house at night to steal. Can I use private defence?

gold_references.label: Section 35
gold_references.role: general right of private defence of property

acceptable_references.label: Section 41
acceptable_references.reason: right may extend to causing death if the facts amount to house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise

acceptable_references.label: Section 43
acceptable_references.reason: commencement and continuance of right of private defence of property

acceptable_references.label: Section 37
acceptable_references.reason: sets restrictions on the right of private defence

required_points: Section 35 provides the general right of private defence of property against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, and attempts to commit those offences.
If someone enters a house at night to steal, private defence of property may apply, subject to the restrictions in Section 37.
optional_points: The right commences when there is a reasonable apprehension of danger to property (Section 43).
Section 41 may become relevant if the facts amount to house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, where private defence of property can extend to causing death.
The right is still subject to not exceeding what is necessary.
forbidden_points: Private defence of property can never extend to causing death in any case.
The right extends to causing death for any theft, not just night-time house-breaking.

notes: Scenario query. Section 35 is primary because the user asks whether private defence can apply; Section 41 is a stronger consequence only if the facts fit house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise.

query: A group planned to commit an offence but was caught before doing it. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 61
gold_references.role: criminal conspiracy - agreement to commit illegal act

acceptable_references.label: Section 62
acceptable_references.reason: attempt provisions may apply if any act towards the offence was done

required_points: Section 61 defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to do or cause to be done an illegal act or an act not illegal by illegal means.
The group may be charged with criminal conspiracy even if the offence was not committed.
Where the conspiracy is to commit an offence, no overt act beyond the agreement is required.
optional_points: If any act was done in furtherance of the plan, attempt under Section 62 may also apply.
forbidden_points: No offence is committed until the planned act is executed.
Criminal conspiracy requires the offence to be fully committed.

notes: Scenario query applying Section 61 criminal conspiracy.

query: Someone encouraged another person to commit theft. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 45
gold_references.role: abetment by instigation

acceptable_references.label: Section 49
acceptable_references.reason: applies if the theft abetted is committed in consequence and no express punishment is provided

acceptable_references.label: Section 56
acceptable_references.reason: punishment for abetment of an offence punishable with imprisonment where the offence is not committed

required_points: Section 45 provides that a person who instigates another to do a thing abets that thing.
Encouraging another person to commit theft amounts to abetment by instigation.
If the theft is committed in consequence of the abetment, Section 49 applies and the abettor is liable to the same punishment as for the offence.
optional_points: If the theft is not committed, Section 56 may apply providing for reduced punishment.
forbidden_points: Encouraging another to commit a crime is not an offence unless the person actually commits the crime.
The person encouraging can only be tried if present at the scene.

notes: Scenario query applying Section 45 (abetment by instigation).

query: A person knowingly bought stolen property. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 317
gold_references.role: receiving stolen property knowing it to be stolen

required_points: Section 317(2) provides that whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen property, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both.
Knowledge or reason to believe the property is stolen is essential.
optional_points: If the stolen property was obtained through dacoity, enhanced punishment under Section 317(3) applies.
forbidden_points: Buying property without knowledge it is stolen is an offence.
The punishment for receiving stolen property is the same as robbery.

notes: Scenario query applying Section 317.

query: A servant stole property from their employer. What section may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 306
gold_references.role: theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

acceptable_references.label: Section 303
acceptable_references.reason: underlying theft definition

required_points: Section 306 provides that whoever, being a clerk or servant, or being employed in the capacity of a clerk or servant, commits theft in respect of any property in the possession of their master or employer, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and also be liable to fine.
This is a specific and more severely punished form of theft applicable to the employer-servant relationship.
forbidden_points: A servant who steals from their employer can only be charged under general theft under Section 303.
The punishment is the same as ordinary theft.

notes: Scenario query. Section 306 is the specific provision for servant theft.

query: Someone threatened to kill me unless I paid money. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 308
gold_references.role: extortion - putting person in fear and inducing delivery of property

acceptable_references.label: Section 351
acceptable_references.reason: criminal intimidation may also apply if money was not actually delivered

required_points: Threatening to kill unless money is paid and thereby inducing delivery of property constitutes extortion under Section 308.
Section 308(5) provides that extortion by putting a person in fear of death or grievous hurt is punishable with imprisonment up to ten years and fine.
If money was not actually delivered but the threat was made to cause alarm or force an act, criminal intimidation under Section 351 may also apply.
forbidden_points: This is only criminal intimidation and not extortion.
The offence is robbery because a threat to kill was used.

notes: Scenario query. Extortion under Section 308 is the primary provision.

query: Someone spread a false statement to damage my reputation. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 356
gold_references.role: defamation - making imputation intending to harm reputation

required_points: Section 356 defines defamation as making or publishing any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing it likely to harm, the reputation of such person.

The imputation must lower the moral or intellectual character of the person in the estimation of others, lower their character in respect of caste or calling, lower their credit, or cause the person's body to be believed in a loathsome state.
Spreading a false statement to damage reputation may amount to defamation.
optional_points: Section 356 has several exceptions; the final determination depends on whether any exception applies.
forbidden_points: Defamation only applies to written statements.
Truth can never be a defence to defamation.

notes: Scenario query. Section 356 for defamation.

query: A person gave false evidence in court. What offence is this?

gold_references.label: Section 227
gold_references.role: definition of giving false evidence

acceptable_references.label: Section 229
acceptable_references.reason: punishment for giving or fabricating false evidence

required_points: Section 227 defines giving false evidence as making a false statement while legally bound by oath or express provision of law to state the truth.
Section 229(1) provides that intentionally giving false evidence in any stage of a judicial proceeding is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine up to ten thousand rupees.
forbidden_points: Giving false evidence in court is not covered by BNS.
False testimony is only an offence if a conviction results.

notes: Scenario query. Section 227 is primary because the query asks what offence it is; Section 229 is acceptable for punishment.

query: Someone forged a document to claim property. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 336
gold_references.role: forgery - making false document to support a claim or title

acceptable_references.label: Section 338
acceptable_references.reason: forgery of valuable security, will, or property authority - enhanced punishment

acceptable_references.label: Section 335
acceptable_references.reason: defines what constitutes making a false document

required_points: Section 336 defines forgery as making a false document with intent to cause damage or injury, to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property.
Making a forged document to claim property clearly falls within this definition.
If the forged document purports to be a will or valuable security, the enhanced punishment provisions of Section 338 apply.
optional_points: Using the forged document as genuine would additionally attract Section 340.
forbidden_points: Forging a document to claim property is only cheating, not forgery.
Forgery requires use of a printing press.

notes: Scenario query. Section 336 for forgery, Section 338 if document is will or security.

query: A person used a fake seal to create a legal-looking document. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 341
gold_references.role: making or possessing counterfeit seal with intent to commit forgery

acceptable_references.label: Section 336
acceptable_references.reason: forgery is the underlying offence

acceptable_references.label: Section 338
acceptable_references.reason: if the document relates to valuable security or will

required_points: Section 341 provides that whoever makes or counterfeits any seal, plate or other instrument for making an impression intending it for committing forgery punishable under Section 338, or possesses such instrument knowing it to be counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to seven years, and also fine.
Using a fake seal to create a legal-looking document also constitutes forgery under Section 336.
forbidden_points: Using a fake seal is only a minor infraction.
Only government officials can commit seal-related forgery offences.

notes: Scenario query. Section 341 is specifically about counterfeit seals.

query: Someone obstructed a public road and caused danger. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 285
gold_references.role: causing danger or obstruction in public way

required_points: Section 285 provides that whoever, by doing any act or by omitting to take order with any property in possession or charge, causes danger, obstruction or injury to any person in any public way or public line of navigation, shall be punished with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees.
forbidden_points: Obstructing a public road is not an offence under BNS.
The punishment for obstructing a public road is imprisonment.

notes: Scenario query. Section 285.

query: A person negligently spread a dangerous infection. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 271
gold_references.role: negligent act likely to spread infection of dangerous disease

acceptable_references.label: Section 272
acceptable_references.reason: malignant act spreading infection - applicable if done maliciously

required_points: Section 271 provides that whoever unlawfully or negligently does any act which is, and which they know or have reason to believe to be, likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life, shall be punished with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.
The act must be negligent and the person must know or have reason to believe it is likely to spread dangerous disease.
optional_points: If the act is done malignantly (intentionally), Section 272 applies with enhanced punishment of imprisonment up to two years.
forbidden_points: Negligent spreading of disease is not an offence under BNS.
The punishment is always imprisonment for two years.

notes: Scenario query. Section 271 for negligent spreading; Section 272 if malignant.

query: Is life imprisonment always for whole life or can it mean fixed years?

gold_references.label: Section 6
gold_references.role: life imprisonment reckoned as twenty years for calculation purposes unless otherwise provided

gold_references.label: Section 4
gold_references.role: lists imprisonment for life as a punishment under BNS

acceptable_references.label: Section 64
acceptable_references.reason: example provision that can specify imprisonment for the remainder of natural life

acceptable_references.label: Section 65
acceptable_references.reason: example provision that can specify imprisonment for the remainder of natural life

acceptable_references.label: Section 70
acceptable_references.reason: example provision that can specify imprisonment for the remainder of natural life

acceptable_references.label: Section 71
acceptable_references.reason: example provision for repeat offenders punished with imprisonment for the remainder of natural life

wrong_references.label: Section 62
wrong_references.reason: attempt provision, not the main rule for life imprisonment duration

required_points: Life imprisonment is not always exactly twenty years or always the whole natural life; the answer depends on the context.
Section 6 provides that for calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life is reckoned as equivalent to twenty years unless otherwise provided.

Several provisions expressly specify that imprisonment for life means imprisonment for the remainder of the person's natural life (e.g., Section 71 for repeat sex offenders, Sections 65, 70, and certain others).
optional_points: The twenty-year equivalence in Section 6 is only for fraction-calculation purposes, not a cap on actual imprisonment.
forbidden_points: Life imprisonment always means exactly twenty years.
Life imprisonment always means the whole natural life in every case.
Section 62 is the main rule for the meaning of life imprisonment.

notes: Multi-hop query. Section 6 is the required rule; natural-life provisions such as Sections 64, 65, 70, and 71 are acceptable examples rather than mandatory citations.

query: If a crime is committed on an Indian aircraft outside India, does BNS apply?

gold_references.label: Section 1(5)(b)
gold_references.role: BNS applies to any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be

required_points: Yes. Section 1(5)(b) provides that the provisions of BNS shall also apply to any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India, wherever it may be.
Therefore, an offence committed on an Indian-registered aircraft outside India falls within the scope of BNS.
forbidden_points: BNS does not apply to offences outside India in any case.
The aircraft must be within Indian airspace for BNS to apply.

notes: Multi-hop query requiring Section 1(5)(b).

query: If an Indian citizen commits an offence outside India, can BNS apply?

gold_references.label: Section 1(5)(a)
gold_references.role: BNS applies to any citizen of India in any place outside India

required_points: Yes. Section 1(5)(a) provides that the provisions of BNS shall apply to any citizen of India in any place outside India.
The illustration in Section 1 gives the example that A, a citizen of India who commits murder in any place outside India, can be tried and convicted in India.
forbidden_points: BNS never applies outside India.
BNS applies outside India only to government employees.

notes: Multi-hop query. Section 1(5)(a) is the applicable provision.

query: If someone commits an act by mistake of fact, can they be protected?

gold_references.label: Section 14
gold_references.role: act done by mistake of fact believing oneself bound by law

acceptable_references.label: Section 17
acceptable_references.reason: act done by mistake of fact believing oneself justified by law

required_points: Section 14 protects a person who, by reason of a mistake of fact (not mistake of law) and in good faith, believes themselves to be bound by law to do the act.
The protection is only for mistakes of fact, not mistakes of law.
The act must be done in good faith, meaning with due care and attention.
optional_points: Section 17 similarly protects acts done by a person who, by mistake of fact, believes themselves to be justified by law.
forbidden_points: Mistake of fact never provides any protection under BNS.
A mistake of law also provides protection under Section 14.

notes: Multi-hop. Sections 14 and 17 are the relevant provisions.

query: If harm is caused accidentally during a lawful act, is it still an offence?

gold_references.label: Section 18
gold_references.role: accident in doing a lawful act with proper care and caution

required_points: Section 18 provides that nothing is an offence done by accident or misfortune, without criminal intention or knowledge, in doing a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means and with proper care and caution.
All four conditions must be satisfied: lawful act, lawful manner, lawful means, and proper care and caution.
If any of these conditions are absent - for example, if there was want of proper caution - the accident exception does not apply.
forbidden_points: Any accident is excused under BNS.
Harm caused accidentally is always an offence.

notes: Multi-hop query applying Section 18 with all conditions.

query: If an act causes slight harm, is it always punishable?

gold_references.label: Section 33
gold_references.role: acts causing only slight harm not an offence

required_points: Section 33 provides that nothing is an offence by reason that it causes, or is intended to cause, or is known to be likely to cause, any harm, if that harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of such harm.
forbidden_points: Any harm, however slight, is punishable under BNS.
The threshold for harm is subjective and depends on the victim.

notes: Multi-hop query. Section 33 is the de minimis exception.

query: When does private defence start and when does it end?

gold_references.label: Section 40
gold_references.role: commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body

gold_references.label: Section 43
gold_references.role: commencement and continuance of right of private defence of property

acceptable_references.label: Section 37
acceptable_references.reason: restrictions on private defence including when public authority can be approached

required_points: Section 40 provides that the right of private defence of body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence, even though the offence may not have been committed; and continues as long as the apprehension of danger continues.

Section 43 provides that the right of private defence of property commences when a reasonable apprehension of danger to the property commences; and continues in different ways depending on whether the threat is theft, robbery, or trespass.
optional_points: The right ends when the apprehension of danger ends or when public authority assistance becomes available.
forbidden_points: Private defence can only start after the first blow is struck.
Private defence continues indefinitely after an attack.

notes: Multi-hop query requiring both Section 40 and Section 43.

query: Can private defence be used against a public servant?

gold_references.label: Section 37
gold_references.role: no right of private defence against public servant acting in good faith under colour of office

acceptable_references.label: Section 35
acceptable_references.reason: general scope of right of private defence

required_points: Section 37 provides that there is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or grievous hurt, if done or attempted to be done by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, even if that act may not be strictly justifiable by law.
However, if the act by a public servant does reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt, the right of private defence may still be exercised.
forbidden_points: Private defence can always be used against a public servant.
There is never any right of private defence against a public servant.

notes: Multi-hop. Section 37 limits private defence against public servants acting in good faith.

query: Can a person be punished for both abetment and the offence committed?

gold_references.label: Section 52
gold_references.role: abettor liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and act done

acceptable_references.label: Section 49
acceptable_references.reason: general punishment of abetment when act is committed

required_points: Section 52 provides that if the act for which the abettor is liable is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitutes a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences.
Therefore, a person can be punished cumulatively for both abetment and the additional offence committed.
optional_points: For example, if A instigates B to resist a distress and B, in offering resistance, voluntarily causes grievous hurt to an officer, A is liable for both the abetment of resisting distress and the abetment of grievous hurt.
forbidden_points: A person can never be punished for both abetment and a separate offence.
Punishment can only be given for the more serious of the two offences.

notes: Multi-hop. Section 52 allows cumulative punishment.

query: Can a person be liable if the abetted act causes a different result than intended?

gold_references.label: Section 53
gold_references.role: abettor liable for different effect if he knew the act was likely to cause it

acceptable_references.label: Section 51
acceptable_references.reason: when different act is done from that abetted, abettor liable if probable consequence

required_points: Section 53 provides that when an act is abetted with a certain intention and causes a different effect from that intended, the abettor is liable for the effect caused in the same manner as if they had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided the abettor knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.
For example, if A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z and Z dies as a result, A is liable for the death if A knew the act was likely to cause death.
forbidden_points: An abettor is only liable for the exact result they intended.
An abettor can never be liable for unintended consequences.

notes: Multi-hop. Section 53 extends abettor liability to unintended but foreseeable effects.

query: What is the difference between theft and robbery?

gold_references.label: Section 303
gold_references.role: definition of theft

gold_references.label: Section 309
gold_references.role: definition of robbery and its relationship to theft

required_points: Section 303 defines theft as dishonestly taking movable property out of a person's possession without consent.

Section 309 provides that theft is robbery if, in order to commit the theft or in committing it or in carrying away the property, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death, hurt, wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint.
The key difference is that robbery involves the use or threat of violence or fear of instant harm, while theft does not.
forbidden_points: Robbery and theft have the same definition.
Robbery requires use of a weapon.

notes: Comparison query. Core difference is use of force/fear of instant harm.

query: What is the difference between robbery and dacoity?

gold_references.label: Section 309
gold_references.role: definition of robbery

gold_references.label: Section 310
gold_references.role: definition of dacoity

required_points: Robbery under Section 309 involves theft or extortion using violence or fear of instant harm, and can be committed by one or more persons.

Dacoity under Section 310 is defined as robbery when five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit it, or when the whole number of persons committing, attempting, or aiding amounts to five or more.
The essential distinction is the number of persons: five or more conjointly makes it dacoity.
forbidden_points: Dacoity requires use of deadly weapons.
Any theft by a group of people is dacoity.

notes: Comparison query. Number of persons (5 or more) is the key distinction.

query: What is the difference between wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement?

gold_references.label: Section 126
gold_references.role: definition of wrongful restraint

gold_references.label: Section 127
gold_references.role: definition of wrongful confinement

required_points: Section 126 defines wrongful restraint as obstructing a person from proceeding in any direction in which they have a right to proceed.
Section 127 defines wrongful confinement as restraining a person in such a manner as to prevent them from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits.
The key difference is that wrongful restraint prevents movement in one or some directions, while wrongful confinement prevents movement beyond a circumscribed area in all directions.
forbidden_points: Wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement are the same offence.
Wrongful confinement requires use of physical force.

notes: Comparison query. Restraint = blocked direction; Confinement = enclosed within limits.

query: What is the difference between hurt and grievous hurt?

gold_references.label: Section 114
gold_references.role: definition of hurt

gold_references.label: Section 116
gold_references.role: definition and enumeration of grievous hurt

required_points: Section 114 defines hurt as causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person.

Section 116 designates only specific kinds of hurt as grievous, including emasculation, permanent privation of sight or hearing, privation of a member or joint, permanent disfiguration, fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth, and hurt that endangers life or causes fifteen days of severe pain or inability to pursue ordinary pursuits.
Grievous hurt is a more severe form; only the kinds listed in Section 116 qualify.
forbidden_points: Any serious injury is grievous hurt.
Grievous hurt and hurt are treated identically under BNS.

notes: Comparison query. Section 116 provides an exhaustive list of grievous hurt.

query: What is the difference between murder and culpable homicide?

gold_references.label: Section 100
gold_references.role: definition of culpable homicide

gold_references.label: Section 101
gold_references.role: definition of murder and exceptions

acceptable_references.label: Section 105
acceptable_references.reason: punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

required_points: Section 100 defines culpable homicide as causing death with intention to cause death, intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death, or knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

Section 101 provides that culpable homicide is murder if the act is done with intention to cause death; or intention to cause bodily injury that the offender knows to be likely to cause death of that person; or intention to cause bodily injury and such injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; or with knowledge that the act is imminently dangerous and must in all probability cause death.

Murder is culpable homicide with the higher degree of intention or knowledge; culpable homicide not amounting to murder involves a lesser degree of intention or falls within exceptions listed in Section 101.
optional_points: Section 101 lists five exceptions where culpable homicide is not murder.
forbidden_points: Murder and culpable homicide are the same offence.
Culpable homicide is always a lesser punishment than murder.

notes: Comparison query. The distinction is one of degree of intention and knowledge.

query: What is the difference between cheating and criminal breach of trust?

gold_references.label: Section 318
gold_references.role: definition of cheating

gold_references.label: Section 316
gold_references.role: definition of criminal breach of trust

required_points: Section 318 defines cheating as deceiving a person to fraudulently or dishonestly induce delivery of property or causing that person to do or omit something to their detriment.
Section 316 defines criminal breach of trust as being entrusted with property and dishonestly misappropriating, converting or disposing of it in violation of a direction of law or a legal contract.
The key difference is that cheating involves deception to obtain property; criminal breach of trust involves dishonest misuse of property that was lawfully entrusted.
forbidden_points: Cheating and criminal breach of trust are the same offence.
Criminal breach of trust requires deception at the time of receiving property.

notes: Comparison query. Deception (cheating) vs dishonest misuse of entrusted property (CBT).

query: What is the difference between abetment and criminal conspiracy?

gold_references.label: Section 45
gold_references.role: definition of abetment

gold_references.label: Section 61
gold_references.role: definition of criminal conspiracy

required_points: Section 45 defines abetment as instigating, engaging in conspiracy for, or intentionally aiding the doing of a thing; it can be by a single person and does not necessarily require an agreement.

Section 61 defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to do or cause to be done an illegal act or an act not illegal by illegal means; it requires at least two persons and is the agreement itself that is the offence.

Abetment is broader; conspiracy is a specific type of abetment involving an agreement between two or more persons. Criminal conspiracy can be charged independently even without any further act in some cases.
forbidden_points: Abetment and criminal conspiracy are the same.
Criminal conspiracy can be committed by one person.

notes: Comparison query. Key differences: number of persons and the role of agreement.

query: What is the difference between criminal force and assault?

gold_references.label: Section 129
gold_references.role: definition of criminal force

gold_references.label: Section 130
gold_references.role: definition of assault

required_points: Section 129 defines criminal force as intentionally using force on a person without consent in order to commit an offence or to cause injury, fear or annoyance.
Section 130 defines assault as making any gesture or preparation intending or knowing it likely to cause any person present to apprehend that criminal force is about to be used against them.
The key difference is that criminal force involves actual application of force, while assault involves only an apprehension or threat of force without actual contact.
optional_points: Mere words cannot constitute assault under Section 130.
forbidden_points: Assault requires actual physical contact.
Criminal force and assault are identical offences.

notes: Comparison query. Assault = apprehension; Criminal force = actual application of force.

query: What is the difference between defamation and insult?

gold_references.label: Section 356
gold_references.role: definition of defamation

gold_references.label: Section 352
gold_references.role: intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

required_points: Section 356 defines defamation as making or publishing any imputation concerning a person intending to harm, or knowing it likely to harm, their reputation.

Section 352 deals with intentional insult which gives provocation to any person, intending or knowing it likely that such provocation will cause the person to break the public peace or commit an offence.
Defamation is directed at harming reputation; insult under Section 352 is directed at provoking a breach of public peace. They are distinct offences with different elements.
forbidden_points: Defamation and insult are the same offence.
Insult always amounts to defamation.

notes: Comparison query. Defamation harms reputation; insult under S.352 aims at provocation.

query: What is the difference between kidnapping and abduction?

gold_references.label: Section 137
gold_references.role: definition of kidnapping

gold_references.label: Section 138
gold_references.role: definition of abduction

required_points: Section 137 defines kidnapping as either conveying a person beyond the limits of India without consent (kidnapping from India) or taking or enticing a child or person of unsound mind out of the keeping of their lawful guardian without the guardian's consent (kidnapping from lawful guardianship).
Section 138 defines abduction as compelling or inducing by force or deceitful means any person to go from any place.

Kidnapping requires the person to be a minor or of unsound mind (for guardianship kidnapping) or the act to be beyond India's limits; abduction applies to any person regardless of age and requires force or deceit.
forbidden_points: Kidnapping and abduction are the same offence.
Abduction only applies to children.

notes: Comparison query. Key differences: age/status of victim, consent of guardian, crossing limits.

query: Give a simple example of theft under BNS.

gold_references.label: Section 303
gold_references.role: definition and illustrations of theft

required_points: Section 303 provides examples in its illustrations: A, being Z's servant and entrusted with Z's plate, dishonestly runs away with the plate without Z's consent - A has committed theft.
The essential elements are: dishonest intention to take, movable property, out of another's possession, without consent.
optional_points: Another illustration: A cuts down a tree on Z's ground with intention of dishonestly taking it - once the tree is severed, A has committed theft.
forbidden_points: Taking property with the owner's permission is theft.
Any removal of property, even without dishonest intent, is theft.

notes: Illustration query. Should use examples from Section 303 illustrations.

query: Give an example where taking property is not theft.

gold_references.label: Section 303
gold_references.role: illustrations showing when taking property is not theft

required_points: Section 303 illustrations include: A, in good faith, believing property belonging to Z to be A's own property, takes it out of Z's possession - as A does not take dishonestly, A does not commit theft.
Another example from Section 303: A finds a ring lying on the highroad not in anyone's possession - A by taking it commits no theft (though may commit criminal misappropriation).
Taking property openly and with belief of entitlement, or with implied consent, is not theft because dishonest intent is absent.
forbidden_points: Any taking of another's property is always theft.
Good faith is irrelevant to whether an act is theft.

notes: Illustration query. Good faith belief of ownership, or absence of dishonest intent, prevents theft.

query: Explain private defence with a simple example.

gold_references.label: Section 34
gold_references.role: acts done in private defence are not offences

gold_references.label: Section 36
gold_references.role: illustration of private defence against a person of unsound mind

acceptable_references.label: Section 35
acceptable_references.reason: scope of right of private defence of body and property

required_points: Section 34 provides that nothing done in the exercise of the right of private defence is an offence.

Section 36 provides an illustration: Z, a person of unsound mind, attempts to kill A. Z is guilty of no offence. But A has the same right of private defence against Z which A would have if Z were sane.
optional_points: Another example: if someone attacks you with a fist, you may use proportionate force to defend yourself; you do not commit an offence.
forbidden_points: Private defence allows unlimited retaliation.
Private defence only applies to defend against threats to life.

notes: Illustration query. Should use examples from the BNS illustrations, particularly Section 36.

query: Explain good faith with a simple example.

gold_references.label: Section 2(11)
gold_references.role: definition of good faith - requires due care and attention

acceptable_references.label: Section 14
acceptable_references.reason: illustration of good faith in mistaken belief of legal duty

acceptable_references.label: Section 27
acceptable_references.reason: illustration of act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind

required_points: Section 2(11) defines good faith as requiring due care and attention; nothing is done in good faith without due care and attention.

Section 14 provides an illustration: A, an officer of a Court, ordered to arrest Y, and after due enquiry believing Z to be Y, arrests Z. A has committed no offence because A acted in good faith with due care.
forbidden_points: Good faith means any honest belief, even one formed carelessly.
Good faith requires the person to be a professional.

notes: Illustration query. Good faith requires due care; illustrations from Section 14.

query: Explain consent under fear with a simple example.

gold_references.label: Section 28
gold_references.role: consent under fear or misconception is not valid consent

required_points: Section 28 provides that consent given under fear of injury or under a misconception of fact is not valid consent if the person doing the act knows or has reason to believe the consent was given in consequence of such fear or misconception.
Example: if A tells Z that Z's life is in danger unless Z signs a document, and Z signs out of fear, that consent is not valid under Section 28.
forbidden_points: Consent given under any pressure is always valid.
Only physical coercion invalidates consent under BNS.

notes: Illustration query. Section 28 requires fear or misconception to be known to the doer.
